title: The Power Of Gatekeeping
description: Controlling access to a person, resource, or information gives you immense power. Gatekeepers are the people you must pass through to get what you need. They can grant or deny opportunity, often in ways that serve their own status.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Controlling access to a person, resource, or information gives you immense power. Gatekeepers are the people you must pass through to get what you need. They can grant or deny opportunity, often in ways that serve their own status.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: An executive assistant decides who gets on the boss’s calendar, and in what order. They can make you wait weeks or squeeze you in tomorrow.
A senior partner decides which junior gets the high‑visibility case. Favoritism, not merit, rules.
A hiring manager is the only route into a company. They slow‑walk candidates they don’t personally like, regardless of qualifications.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Creating unnecessary steps: “I’ll have to run it by…”
Selective information sharing: “You didn’t hear about the deadline change?”
Making themselves indispensable: no one else has the password, the contact list, or the process.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “Let me see if he’s available.” (when she knows he is)
“I’ll put in a good word for you.” (implying your success depends on them)
“I’m afraid that’s not possible right now.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: A person who seems to control all access and enjoys reminding you of it.
You feel like you’re begging for something that should be routine.
The gatekeeper’s mood determines whether things get done.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Gatekeeping is a form of structural power. By controlling a bottleneck, the gatekeeper can extract favors, deference, and status from those who need passage. It’s a classic bureaucratic power move.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Build a relationship with the gatekeeper before you need something. Acknowledge their role and treat them with genuine respect.
If possible, find an alternative route: go around them, but carefully, because going around can make an enemy.
If you are the leader, break the bottleneck: set clear criteria for access, so it’s not based on personal whim.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Treating gatekeepers as obstacles rather than as people with their own goals. Understand what they want, and you can often align.
Assuming the gatekeeper is just following orders; they often have more discretion than they appear.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A consultant needs five minutes with a CEO to pitch a million‑dollar idea. The CEO’s assistant tells her, “His schedule is full for months.” The consultant sends the assistant a thank‑you gift and a note saying, “I know how hard your job is; I’d appreciate any guidance on the best way to reach him.” The assistant finds a 10‑minute slot next week. The deal closes.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The drawbridge keeper may not own the castle, but they decide who enters. Bow to the keeper—not in submission, but in recognition of their power to open or close.
